name: Gua sha

card.summary: A scraping massage with a smooth jade, stone or steel tool, used on the face to reduce morning puffiness and sharpen the look of the jawline and cheekbones.
card.note: Body-style gua sha deliberately raises bruise-like marks; facial versions use lighter pressure.

quick.overview:
Gua sha is a traditional East Asian technique in which a smooth-edged tool is stroked across oiled skin. In looksmaxxing and skincare circles the facial version is used to move fluid out of the face in the morning, so the jawline, cheekbones and under-eyes look leaner and less swollen.

The practice is centuries old in traditional Chinese medicine, and facial use spread widely on social media around 2021 to 2022. Small studies have measured skin blood flow after scraping and compared gua sha with a facial roller over eight weeks; larger trials of cosmetic claims are limited.
quick.how: Users cleanse the face, apply oil or moisturiser for glide, then draw a flat jade, rose quartz or steel tool along the jaw, cheeks and forehead with light pressure, usually in upward and outward strokes, for several minutes. Forum users pair it with ice, cold water and low-sodium habits as a morning de-bloating routine. Tools are kept clean between uses.
quick.risks: Body gua sha is designed to produce red or purple petechiae and bruising, and reviews list redness, bruising, dermatitis and, with unclean tools, infection risk. Rare severe injuries are described in dermatology literature. Facial routines use lighter pressure; people on blood thinners or with fragile skin, rosacea or active acne are generally cautioned by clinicians.

lead: Gua sha is a traditional East Asian technique in which a smooth tool, historically a spoon, coin or piece of horn and now often jade, rose quartz or steel, is stroked across lubricated skin.[1][2] In looksmaxxing and skincare communities it is used on the face as a manual de-bloating and contouring routine: the goal is to reduce morning puffiness and make the jawline, cheekbones and eye area look more defined.[3][4]

Traditionally the technique is applied firmly to the back, neck and limbs until sha, temporary red or purple marks, appear, and it is practiced under names such as cao gio in Vietnam and coining elsewhere.[1][5] Facial versions use lighter pressure and are not meant to leave marks.[1] Their popularity grew sharply on TikTok and other platforms in 2021 and 2022.[1]

Researchers have studied the body technique mostly for pain, and a small number of studies have looked at skin microcirculation and facial outcomes.[6][7][8] Dermatology commentators describe the cosmetic claims, such as lymphatic drainage, as largely based on tradition and small studies.[9]

chain: Oiled skin is stroked with a smooth tool along the jaw and cheeks
Temporary increase in local blood flow and manual fluid movement
Less puffiness and a more defined jawline and cheekbones in the short term
angle.text: People use gua sha as a morning routine to look less swollen in the face, aiming at a sharper jaw and cheek outline and brighter skin. Looksmaxxers often combine it with cold exposure and diet changes aimed at facial water retention.

paras: Gua sha means roughly scraping to produce sha, the reddish marks that appear when pressure is drawn over the skin. Practitioners apply oil or balm, then make firm, mostly one-directional strokes along muscle groups or traditional meridians with a smooth-edged tool.[1] It is often practiced alongside cupping in traditional Chinese medicine.[1][11]

Facial gua sha uses shaped boards, usually jade or quartz, and lighter pressure. Strokes typically travel from the centre of the face outward and upward, and along the jaw and neck.[1] The looksmax.org guide to jade gua sha describes benefits including improved circulation, less puffiness and a more chiselled face, and advises oil to reduce friction.[12]

Wikipedia notes that similar scraping with stones may go back to prehistory, and that formal use in traditional Chinese medicine is described from the Ming dynasty.[1] The related Vietnamese practice cao gio and coining traditions in Southeast Asia brought the marks to Western clinicians' attention, and a 2018 JAMA Dermatology article describes gua sha, or coining therapy, for dermatology readers.[5]

The facial trend took off on social media in 2021 and 2022, when beauty influencers promoted it for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation.[1] Forum threads on looksmax.org discuss whether tools are necessary or whether hands and other objects can substitute.[13]

Proponents say gua sha boosts circulation, relaxes tense facial and neck muscles, moves lymph fluid and reduces puffiness, helping skin look brighter and more contoured.[12][4] On looksmax.org, some users treat it as part of a de-bloating toolkit with ice and diet; others question whether it is a placebo-like routine.[3][15]

A pilot study in healthy volunteers found that gua sha increased surface microcirculation of the treated area, which the authors proposed as a mechanism behind its pain-relieving effects.[7] Randomised trials have mostly examined body use, for instance chronic low back pain and neck pain, with reports of reduced pain compared with waitlist or control groups.[8][16][17] A systematic review has also examined gua sha for perimenopausal symptoms.[18]

For the face, an 8-week randomised trial of 34 women aged 20 to 50 compared facial roller and gua sha massage (10 minutes, five days a week) on facial contour, muscle tone and skin elasticity measurements.[6] A 2023 dermatology letter reviews gua sha, jade rollers and facial massage and discusses what benefits they might offer, and a 2009 review addresses research language around gua sha.[9][19]

Reviewers note that body gua sha nearly always causes some skin trauma such as redness or bruising, and minor burns, dermatitis or blood in the urine have been reported; rare severe injuries, including brain bleeds and wounds requiring grafts, appear in the literature.[1][5] Safety protocols for gua sha and cupping emphasise clean tools and avoiding broken skin.[11] Because tools contact skin, hygiene matters, a point also raised by forum users.[13]
Some reviewers, including Edzard Ernst, classify the practice as lacking high-quality evidence for its therapeutic claims.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org facial gua sha is discussed as a morning de-bloating and jaw-definition tool, alongside questions about whether tools are needed and whether it overlaps with icing.[3][13][15]

claims.claim: Gua sha gives a more 'chiselled' face
claims.believers: Guide authors say regular use improves circulation, reduces puffiness and defines the face.[12]
claims.experts: An 8-week randomised trial compared gua sha with a facial roller on facial contour and skin measures; the literature on lasting contour change is small.[6][9]

claims.claim: It drains lymph and reduces puffiness
claims.believers: Users describe less morning swelling after a session.[12][3]
claims.experts: Studies report increased local microcirculation after scraping; lymphatic drainage claims have not been directly measured in published trials cited here.[7][9]

claims.believers: One user says non-clean substitutes cause breakouts, another asks whether cleaning is enough.[13]
claims.experts: Safety protocols stress clean tools and intact skin.[11]
